plain_english: Keep this thought ready: when you lose something external, ask what you gain instead. If what you gain is worth more, never say you've suffered a loss. You wouldn't say that if you got a horse instead of a donkey, or an ox instead of a sheep. Same goes for getting a good deed instead of money, or proper calm instead of pointless chatter, or modesty instead of crude talk. Remember this, and you'll always keep your character where it should be.
original_excerpt: Keep this thought in readiness, when you lose anything external, what you acquire in place of it; and if it be worth more, never say, I have had a loss; neither if you have got a horse in place of an ass, or an ox in place of a sheep, nor a good action in place of a bit of money, nor in place of idle talk such tranquillity as befits a man, nor in place of lewd talk if you have acquired modesty. If you remember this, you will always maintain your character such as it ought to be.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things, Section 1

plain_english: If you don't pay attention, remember this: your chances are slipping away. Whatever effort you've put into improving yourself will be wasted and destroyed. It takes very little to lose everything you've worked for — just a tiny slip from sound thinking. A ship's captain doesn't need much to wreck his vessel. He needs skill and effort to save it, but to destroy it? He just has to turn the wheel slightly into the wind. The ship is lost. He doesn't even have to do it on purpose — a moment of carelessness is enough. It's the same with your progress. Nod off just a little, and everything you've built up disappears.
original_excerpt: But if you do not, consider that the times of opportunity are perishing, and that whatever pains you take about yourself, you are going to waste them all and overturn them. And it needs only a few things for the loss and overturning of all—namely, a small deviation from reason. For the steerer of a ship to upset it, he has no need of the same means as he has need of for saving it; but if he turns it a little to the wind, it is lost; and if he does not do this purposely, but has been neglecting his duty a little, the ship is lost. Something of the kind happens in this case also; if you only fall a nodding a little, all that you have up to this time collected is gone.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things, Section 1

plain_english: Pay attention to how things appear to you. Watch over your thoughts carefully. What you're protecting isn't small — it's your self-respect, your trustworthiness, your consistency, your emotional calm, your peace of mind, your freedom from fear, your inner quiet. In short, your liberty. What would you sell these things for? Look at what you think you'd get in return. "But won't I get something good for it?" Look closely. If you do get something back, see what you're actually receiving. I have decency, he has a government position. He has a judgeship, I have self-respect. But I don't cheer where it's inappropriate. I won't stand up where I shouldn't. I'm free and a friend of God, so I obey him willingly. But I can't demand anything else — not my body, possessions, political office, good reputation, or anything else. God doesn't let me demand these things. If he wanted them to be good for me, he would have made them so. Since he hasn't, I can't go against his commands. Protect what is truly your own good in everything. As for everything else, handle it as you're allowed to, and only as far as reason permits. Be content with this. If you don't, you'll be miserable. You'll fail at everything. You'll be blocked and obstructed. These are the laws sent from above. These are the orders. You should interpret these laws and submit to them — not to the laws of Masurius and Cassius.
original_excerpt: Attend therefore to the appearances of things, and watch over them; for that which you have to preserve is no small matter, but it is modesty and fidelity and constancy, freedom from the affects, a state of mind undisturbed, freedom from fear, tranquillity, in a word liberty. For what will you sell these things? See what is the value of the things which you will obtain in exchange for these.—But shall I not obtain any such thing for it?—See, and if you do in return get that, see what you receive in place of it. I possess decency, he possesses a tribuneship: he possesses a prætorship, I possess modesty. But I do not make acclamations where it is not becoming: I will not stand up where I ought not; for I am free, and a friend of God. and so I obey him willingly. But I must not claim (seek) anything else, neither body nor possession, nor magistracy, nor good report, nor in fact anything. For he (God) does not allow me to claim (seek) them, for if he had chosen, he would have made them good for me; but he has not done so, and for this reason I cannot transgress his commands. Preserve that which is your own good in everything; and as to every other thing, as it is permitted, and so far as to behave consistently with reason in respect to them, content with this only. If you do not, you will be unfortunate, you will fail in all things, you will be hindered, you will be impeded. These are the laws which have been sent from thence (from God); these are the orders. Of these laws a man ought to be an expositor, to these he ought to submit, not to those of Masurius and Cassius.
source_reference: Discourses, What Things We Should Exchange for Other Things, Section 1
